text: Comparison of Live-Trapping and Noninvasive Genetic Sampling to Assess Patch Occupancy by New England Cottontail (Sylvilagus transitionalis) Rabbits

The New England cottontail (Sylvilagus transitionalis) is a species of high conservation priority in the northeastern United States and a candidate for federal listing under the Endangered Species Act. Eastern cottontails are abundantly distributed and similar in appearance to New England cottontails. Our objective was to compare cost, effort, and effectiveness of live-trapping and noninvasive genetic monitoring for assessing patch occupancy by New England cottontail. We collected 113 tissue samples and 240 fecal pellets samples for diagnostic genetic testing to detect species presence and assess the proportion of samples consisted of New England and eastern cottontail on 5 study sites in Connecticut in 2008 and 2009. Both methods detected presence of New England cottontail at 4 of 5 sites. Overall proportion of DNA samples consisted of New England cottontail was similar between sampling methods (x 2 ¼ 0.189, P ¼ 0.664). However, species composition on individual sites was inconsistent between methods and no clear pattern of bias was discernible. Mean cost per DNA sample to collect and analyze was US$433 for tissue samples and US$33 for fecal pellets. Samples collected per person-day of effort were 40 for fecal samples and 0.7 for tissue samples. Genetic monitoring via noninvasive fecal sampling was a low-cost, time-efficient method for assessing species occupancy, but development of an optimal sampling strategy is needed to evaluate composition and distributions of species on sympatrically occupied sites.

Monitoring wildlife populations is critical for effective conservation management, especially for endangered species. Monitoring programs are used to track the responses of species and populations to environmental change, land-use change, habitat modification or disturbance, and to evaluate population persistence. It is also critical to monitor population responses to management action in an adaptive management framework (Nichols and Williams 2006).
Increasingly, monitoring is conducted with noninvasive genetic sampling approaches, which use the DNA extracted from hair, feces, feathers or other biological samples collected without capturing, handling, or observing the animal of interest (reviewed in Waits and Paetkau 2005). This approach is particularly advantageous for monitoring rare, elusive, or endangered species for which field-based methods are logistically challenging, and minimizing disturbance to the animals is desirable (Kohn andWayne 1997, Creel et al. 2003). Few studies have compared noninvasive genetic sampling with other monitoring approaches based on live animal detections (but see, e.g., Puechmaille andPetit 2007, Ruibal et al. 2009). Comparative studies may reveal biases in methods (Ruibal et al. 2009), although such comparisons may be limited by the fact that rarely is the true population or distribution of animals known. Nonetheless, it is important to know whether different monitoring approaches arrive at similar conclusions, given the obvious implications of monitoring outcomes for conservation management.
Genetic monitoring is commonly used to monitor changes in site occupancy or the geographical range of a species (Schwartz et al. 2007). Knowledge of site occupancy (the proportion of monitoring sites within a region where the species is present) provides useful information to wildlife managers about species distributions and habitat suitability; the presence-absence data can also reflect population status and species abundance (MacKenzie et al. 2005). Occupancy monitoring is germane to the conservation management of the New England cottontail (Sylvilagus transitionalis), a candidate for federal listing under the Endangered Species Act and one of the species of greatest conservation need in the northeastern United States (USFWS 2006(USFWS , 2009)).
Once widespread throughout New England and eastern New York, populations of New England cottontail have declined dramatically throughout the region (Chapman and Stauffer 1981, Litvaitis et al. 2006, Tash and Litvaitis 2007). Remaining New England cottontails occur in 5 geographically distinct populations within about 14% of their historical range (90,000 km 2 ; Litvaitis et al. 2006). Two of 5 distinct New England cottontail populations occupy eastern and western Connecticut, USA. The decline was attributed primarily to the loss and fragmentation of the early successional (thicket) habitat on which this species depends (Litvaitis andVillafuerte 1996, Litvaitis et al. 2008). Chapman and Morgan (1973) also suggested that declining New England cottontail populations were partially attributed to increased competition from the more adaptable eastern cottontail (S. floridanus). Eastern cottontails are similar in appearance to New England cottontails, and were introduced into the Northeast United States in the 1920s (Dice 1927). The species are sympatric within a large portion of the New England cottontail's range (Litvaitis et al. 2006) and have been documented to have overlapping home ranges in the same habitat patch (Goodie et al. 2004). Although both species may occupy the same habitat patches, there is no evidence to suggest that hybridization occurs between New England and eastern cottontails (Litvaitis et al. 1997). Overlap in spatial distribution and morphological similarities between New England and eastern cottontails make it difficult to confirm patch occupancy by species.
Several approaches exist for distinguishing between the 2 species of cottontail, each with their own potential advantages and disadvantages. For dead specimens, skull morphology has been used as a reliable method to differentiate between New England and eastern cottontails (Dalke 1942). For live specimens, a model based on pelage characteristics and body measurements has been used to differentiate between species with 94% reliability (Litvaitis et al. 1991). Genetic tools have also been developed for species identification. A diagnostic mitochondrial DNA assay can reliably differentiate between species (Litvaitis and Litvaitis 1996) and minimizes the uncertainty and observer bias associated with morphological determinations. Species identification of live or dead specimens, therefore, is usually confirmed using genetic testing. This approach requires livetrapping cottontails, typically during winter, or obtaining a fresh mortality. A noninvasive genetic approach based on DNA extracted from fecal pellets also has been used for differentiating between species of lagomorphs (Kovach et al. 2003, Litvaitis et al. 2006, Fenderson et al. 2011). Fecal DNA analysis requires collecting pellets during winter on fresh snow with freezing temperatures to assess species occupancy and distribution (Kovach et al. 2003). Differences in species behavior may influence the effectiveness of livetrapping and noninvasive sampling approaches, which may influence the results obtained by these 2 methods.
Effectiveness of approaches used to identify species of cottontail, and labor and costs associated with each technique, are important considerations when selecting a monitoring approach. No studies have compared effectiveness of sampling approaches for assessing species presence or evaluated cost and effort associated with each approach. Our objective was to compare the cost, effort, and effectiveness of live-trapping and fecal pellet sampling for identifying presence of New England cottontail at sites co-occupied by eastern cottontail.

We collected data on species presence at 5 study sites located in the towns of North Stonington, Scotland, Kent, Morris, and Salem, Connecticut, USA. Previous sampling efforts confirmed that both New England and eastern cottontail species co-occupied all sites (Goodie and Kilpatrick 2007; U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Highway Administration, and Connecticut Department of Transportation 2007). The North Stonington site was a 48ha shelter-wood cut located within a mature hardwood forest. The shelter-wood cut was implemented in 1998 (10 years old at time of study) and was dominated by saplingstage forest with thick patches of greenbrier (Smilax sp.). This area was open to hunting and public access. The Scotland site was a 10-ha patch that consisted of old pasture dominated by multiflora rose (Rosa multiflora) on a private farm. The Kent site was a 16-ha patch consisting of old pastures dominated by briar, vines, and woody shrubs. Small game hunting was permitted but did not take place during this study. The Morris site was a 8-ha patch characterized by grassy areas, abandoned nursery, hedgerows, and hillside thickets surrounded by mature hardwood forest. This area was open to hunting and public access. The Salem site was a 16-ha patch dominated by early succession growth, mainly shrubs and grasses. This site was closed to hunting and public access.

We used live-trapping and fecal pellet sampling in conjunction with genetic testing to detect species presence and assess the proportion of samples consisting of New England and eastern cottontails at 5 study sites. We captured cottontails using Havahart (Woodstream Corp., Lititz, PA) and Tomahawk (Tomahawk Live Trap, Hazelhurst, WI) single-door spring-loaded live-traps (81 cm Â 25 cm Â 31 cm). We deployed 50 traps at each site from January through April over a 2-year period (2008)(2009). A systematic trapping grid was not used to position traps because of the uneven distribution of habitat throughout the patch. Instead, we positioned traps based on distribution and abundance of rabbit sign (browse, tracks, pellets, den sites). We moved traps throughout the patch to areas of activity during the trapping period to maximize trap success. We baited traps with apples and checked traps daily ( 24 hr). No traps were set if heavy rain, freezing rain, or heavy snow was expected. We collected date, location, pelage characteristics, sex, weight, and a tissue sample from each trapped rabbit. We collected tissue samples from the ear tip, placed them in unique 5-ml sterile vials, and immediately froze them to preserve DNA for species identification by genetic testing. We released all rabbits at the site of capture. We collected fecal samples during the same time period that trapping occurred, by traversing all 5 study sites once between January and March. Pellet collection was based on distribution and abundance of rabbit sign, similar to our approach for placing traps. Collection of pellet samples throughout the patch was evenly distributed in areas with rabbit activity. We collected fecal pellets during optimal conditions, on fresh snow cover with temperatures below 08C to minimize DNA degradation (Litvaitis andLitvaitis 1996, Kovach et al. 2003). We collected a single fecal pellet from each pellet group encountered and no pellets were collected in or under traps. We used disposable latex gloves to prevent contamination of fecal samples. Pellets were placed in sterile 15-ml centrifuge tubes and immediately frozen to preserve DNA. Our objective was to collect 40 pellets at each site for analyses. We recorded date and location for each fecal sample collected. We extracted DNA from tissue samples using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) and from fecal pellets using the QIAamp 1 DNA Stool Kit (Qiagen) with minor modifications to the manufacturer's protocol, following Kovach et al. (2003). Fecal pellet extractions were performed in a separate location than tissue extractions. Species identification of both fecal and tissue samples was performed using a combination of 2 diagnostic restriction fragment length polymorphism assays of the mitochondrial control region, following the methods of Litvaitis and Litvaitis (1996) and Kovach et al. (2003). The restriction enzyme BfaI differentiates New England cottontail from eastern cottontail at one diagnostic site (Litvaitis and Litvaitis 1996), while NlaIII not only distinguishes the 2 cottontail species, but also the snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus; Kovach et al. 2003). Because some individual cottontail sequences have other NlaIII sites in addition to the diagnostic sites (A. I. Kovach, unpublished data), we used a combination of both restriction fragment length polymorphism assays for species confirmation. Negative controls (blank samples) were carried through all phases of the process, including extractions, polymerase chain reaction amplifications, and restriction digests, to monitor for contamination. We used chi-square goodness-of-fit test to test for significant differences (P < 0.05) in percent composition of New England and eastern cottontails detected by the 2 different approaches using SYSTAT 12.0 (SYSTAT 2007).
All regulations listed in the Animal Welfare Act (13 May 2002) regarding humane handling, care, and treatment of rabbits were followed. Live-trapping and handling methods were approved by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service and were conducted by experienced personnel.

We collected 113 tissue samples and 240 fecal samples for DNA analysis at 5 locations in Connecticut. Capture success averaged 0.013 rabbits/trap-night and ranged from 0.004 (Morris) to 0.025 (Scotland). Among all sites combined, we captured 48 New England cottontails, 64 eastern cottontails, and 1 unknown cottontail. Both methods detected presence of New England cottontail at 4 of 5 sites and neither method detected presence of New England cottontail at 1 of 5 sites (Salem; Table 1). At the 4 occupied sites, New England cottontail comprised 53% of the sample using tissue DNA and 50% of the sample using fecal DNA. Overall proportion of DNA samples consisting of New England cottontail was similar between sampling strategies (x 2 ¼ 0.189, P ¼ 0.664). Proportion of DNA samples consisting of New England cottontail was not consistent between methods on the individual study sites. We found no difference between sampling methods at the North Stonington site, which generated the largest number of tissue and fecal samples (Table 1). We found differences in proportion of DNA samples consisting of New England cottontail between sampling methods at 3 of 4 remaining sites (Table 1).
Total expenditures for labor, fuel, equipment, and supplies were less for fecal pellet surveys than for live-trapping. Mean cost per sample to collect and analyze was US$432.81 for tissue and US$32.87 for fecal (Table 2). Time required in the field for sample collection was 16 weeks of live-trapping for 113 tissue samples and 3 days of surveying for 240 fecal samples. We were unable to extract amplifiable DNA from 18 of 240 (8%) fecal samples and 1 of 113 (1%) tissue samples to determine species identification.

In the case of the New England cottontail, site occupancy may be a useful metric for current population status and future population persistence. It can also yield valuable information about metapopulation processes, given the ephemeral nature of the early successional habitat on which the species depends (Litvaitis and Villafuerte 1996). The challenges of determining patch occupancy for New England cottontail are exacerbated by their sympatric occurrence with eastern cottontails throughout much of their remaining range. The results of occupancy-monitoring efforts may depend upon the reliability of the methods used; therefore, evaluating the efficiency and reliability of alternative methods is important before incorporating them into an adaptive management program.
Our results indicate that live-trapping and fecal pellet sampling yield similar results for detecting occupancy, but may not yield equivalent conclusions about species composition within a patch. The 2 methods were consistent in detecting presence or absence of New England cottontail on all sites. Overall species composition (as measured by the proportion of trapped individuals or pellet samples confirmed as New England cottontail) pooled among all sites was similar for fecal and tissue DNA collection methods. However, site-specific species composition, as determined by the 2 methods, was significantly different for 3 sites, but neither method consistently favored detection of New England or eastern cottontails. Differences at the patch level (sites) may be due to differences in sampling procedures. Pellet collection occurred on a single day and live-trapping occurred over a 4-month period. Over the extended trapping period, shifts in population composition or movement of individuals from nearby patches may occur. Differences may also be due to sampling artifacts. For example, the percent of samples confirmed as New England cottontail was similar between methods at the North Stonington site, which had the largest sample size, both in terms of the numbers of individuals captured and numbers of pellet samples collected. Both methods failed to detect presence of New England cottontails at the Salem site. Initially, the Salem site was determined to be occupied by New England cottontails, based on DNA confirmation of a fecal pellet in 2005 (U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Highway Administration, and Connecticut Department of Transportation 2007). We suspect that New England cottontails no longer exist at this site or that an established population did not exist in 2005 and the initial sample was from a dispersing individual.
Noninvasive genetic monitoring via fecal pellet sampling relies on the assumption that individuals in the population defecate at the same rate (Kohn et al. 1999). Heterogeneity in defecation rates among age and sex classes or behavioral status can lead to biases in noninvasive monitoring studies (Petit andValiere 2006, Ruibal et al. 2009). Ruibal et al. (2009) found that scat sampling was not as effective as livetrapping for monitoring spotted-tail quoll (Dasyurus maculatus), because it did not yield samples from all individuals monitored via live-trapping over the same time period. Heterogeneity in defecation rates is likely not an influential factor for noninvasive sampling of New England cottontail in the winter, because the population consists of only adult individuals and movements may not be extensive during this nonbreeding period. Nonetheless, there may be sex-specific variation in activity patterns, movements, and defecation rates (Brubaker 2012). Future investigations using molecular sexing and individual identification might be warranted to investigate these potential sex-related biases.
Cost per sample to collect and analyze DNA was 13 times higher for tissue samples collected via live-trapping compared to noninvasive fecal sampling. Similarly, other studies have shown that noninvasive genetic monitoring is more cost-effective than traditional methods based on trapping or radiotelemetry (Schwartz et al. 2007, DeBarba et al. 2010). Although success was greater for extracting quality DNA from tissue samples compared with fecal samples, success for both methods was relatively high. Labor required to sample 5 sites was 27 times higher for collecting tissue samples compared to fecal samples. Number of samples collected per day of effort was 40 for fecal samples and 0.7 for tissue samples.
Noninvasive genetic sampling, to monitor patch occupancy by sympatric populations of cottontails, is a reliable method that required less time, fuel, and equipment compared with live-trapping. Reduced time required to sample sites will provide opportunities to survey more locations. Fecal pellet collection also avoids concerns about possible differences in trap-shyness between species and eliminates concerns about incidental trap mortality.

For sites that may be occupied by both New England and eastern cottontails, fecal pellet sampling provides an efficient alternative to live-trapping to determine occupancy of each species. However, fecal pellet sampling and live-trapping may not yield equivalent results for species composition. Noninvasive collection of fecal pellets alleviates concerns about potential negative impacts of trapping and handling of a threatened species. However, live-trapping can be conducted under a wider array of weather conditions and provides the opportunity to collect additional data from individual rabbits. Further investigation is needed to evaluate the optimal sampling strategy for fecal pellet surveys to accurately assess species composition of eastern and New England cottontails on sympatric patches. Determining this sampling protocol will be important for adaptive management efforts aimed at monitoring population status and response to habitat restoration efforts.
